title: Around the Sea of Galilee

named.name: Capernaum
named.label: above
named.note: Jesus' base in Galilee, "His own town" (9:1). "The house" of 13:1 and 13:36 is probably Peter's (8:14): under the octagonal Byzantine church a first-century house, honoured by early believers, has been excavated. The white limestone synagogue seen today is later, built over the black basalt foundations of an earlier one.

named.name: Nazareth
named.label: below
named.note: His hometown (13:54; 2:23): in the first century a small village in the hills above the Jezreel Valley.

named.name: Gennesaret
named.label: left
named.note: The fertile plain on the north-west shore; Josephus praises its climate and fruit (Jewish War 3.516–521). The "Galilee boat," a fishing boat of the first century, was found in the mud here in 1986.

named.name: Bethsaida
named.label: right
named.site: et-Tell, or el-Araj by the shore
named.note: Luke places the feeding of the 5,000 near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10). Its site is debated: et-Tell, on a hill above the old shoreline, or el-Araj by the lake, where a Byzantine church was found in 2019.

named.name: Tabgha
named.label: below
named.note: The traditional site of the feeding of the 5,000 since the fourth century, with its mosaic of loaves and fishes.

p: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea. Josephus says John was imprisoned and executed at Machaerus, Herod's fortress east of the Dead Sea (Antiquities 18.116–119), well beyond this map. The news sends Jesus to "a solitary place" (14:13).

The lake stood at much the same level in the first century as today, around 209–211 m below sea level: Mendel Nun's survey of the ancient harbours found breakwaters at about −211 to −212 m. The one real change is in the north-east. The Jordan has since carried silt into the bay and built the Beteiha plain, so in Jesus' day the water probably came closer to Bethsaida than the modern shore shows. How much closer is debated, and is part of the argument between et-Tell and el-Araj. The dashed line follows the reconstruction proposed by the Bethsaida Excavations Project geologists (Shroder and others), with a lagoon reaching the foot of et-Tell; it is approximate, and on that view el-Araj would then have been under water. The el-Araj excavators argue instead that their site stood on the first-century shore.

The Sea of Galilee (Kinneret) is about 21 km long and 12 km wide, some 210 m below sea level. Winds funnel down from the surrounding hills, so sudden storms are common, especially in the evening (14:24). The fourth watch (14:25) ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.
